content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Weekly Football Matchup Profiles (MatchupAnalysis_FB2026)

`MatchupAnalysis_FB2026` produces a weekly opponent profile from PFF EPA data, and on 2026-10-03 the Week 5 Baylor–Arizona State profile was generated alongside a Weeks 1–4 backfill. The read was unambiguous in direction and explicitly weak in confidence: ASU's run defense is elite (−0.409 EPA/run, 5th of 138) while its pass defense is merely average (−0.008), and Baylor's run game ranks 120th, so **Baylor has to throw**; ASU's offense ranks 127th and is worst through the air, pointing to a low-scoring game. The profile was flagged "trust lightly" because ASU had played only two FBS games and the previous week's Colorado pass-defense read had not held.

## Key Points

- **The directional conclusion and the confidence in it are reported separately.** A clean rank split (5th-of-138 run defense vs. average pass defense, against a 120th-ranked Baylor run game) supports a tactical read, while a two-FBS-game sample and a failed prior-week read bound how much weight it carries.
- **`pff_game_result.py --season-through N` is now the shared engine for mid-season and post-season analysis,** not just the backfill tool it was written as: Week 6's bye-week mid-season review runs `--season-through 5` plus Big 12 EPA standings, and the post-season version runs `--season-through 12` before the bowl.
- **Its drive-ending tables reconstruct the Week 4 23–13 final score exactly, which functions as a self-check** — a derived output that can be validated against a known ground truth each week rather than trusted on construction.
- **Two inputs are structurally unavailable on Windows.** The CFBD bundle (betting line, SP+, FEI, frozen prediction) cannot be produced because the API key lives only on the Mac, and PFF Ultimate tendencies require a browser — which is what blocks the Keys to Victory, leaving Weeks 3–4 ungraded for want of premium charting rather than for want of plays data.
- **The project lacks a charter,** so `slate-check` keeps flagging `Weekly_Matchups_2026` as DUE; writing one is an estimated five-minute fix.

## Details

The reporting discipline here is the durable part. A matchup profile is a forecast consumed under time pressure before a kickoff, which creates pressure to state a confident read; this one states the read and then names exactly why it might be wrong — opponent sample size, and a concrete prior failure of the same inference class the week before against Colorado. That pairing makes the artifact usable without being overtrusted, and it matches the broader practice in this environment of distinguishing a model's direction from its demonstrated reliability. The frozen-prediction element of the CFBD bundle is what would otherwise convert these weekly reads into a gradeable record, which is why its Mac-only API key is more than an inconvenience: without a pregame capture, the week's read cannot later be scored as genuinely out-of-sample.

The `--season-through N` generalization is a small but consequential architectural result. A script written to backfill prior weeks turned out to be the same computation the mid-season and post-season reviews need, differing only in the cutoff argument, so one engine now serves three cadences instead of three divergent scripts accumulating separate bugs. Its credibility rests on the drive-ending reconstruction: because the tables reproduce the Week 4 23–13 score exactly, a run that fails to reconstruct a known final is evidence of a data or logic fault rather than a judgment call. The open sequence after the ASU game is mechanical — re-pull data, run `pff_game_result.py --week 5`, write the result doc — while the Keys to Victory grader remains blocked on PFF premium charting access and the CFBD bundle remains blocked on being at the Mac. Commits: `5b4cafa` (Week 5) and `4c61641` (backfill).

# Handoff Document Placement: Never Write to /tmp

On 2026-08-15, a session resuming work on the portfolio board project could not locate its handoff document. A search of the entire home directory, six levels deep and excluding `Library` and `node_modules`, turned up nothing. The prior session had written the file to `/tmp/`, which is invisible to a home-directory search and is wiped on reboot. The handoff was copied to `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/project-triage/handoff-portfolio-board-task4-2026-08-15.md`, establishing the rule that handoff documents belong in the project directory. The mistake happened again on 2026-10-14 with the macOS per-user temp folder, which shows the rule has not yet become the default behaviour.

## Key Points

- **`/tmp/` is doubly wrong for handoffs:** the file does not survive a reboot, and it is outside the search path a fresh session would naturally check. Either failure alone loses the document, and together they make the loss silent.
- **The per-user temp folder is the same mistake.** On 2026-10-14 a Cloudroom handoff went to `/var/folders/gw/.../T/handoff-cloudroom-2026-10-14.md`. The session flagged that a reboot could delete it and queued a copy to `~/DEV/Cloudroom_Learning/docs/`. Any OS-managed temp path counts as `/tmp`.
- **Write handoffs into the project directory.** The 10-14 closeout handoff was written correctly to `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/2026-10-14-overnight-catchup.md`, which shows the right placement and the wrong one in sessions only hours apart.
- **When a handoff cannot be found, ask the user for the *project name*, not the file path.** The project name is something the user reliably knows and it localizes the search immediately.
- **A near-limit session should not start work it cannot finish.** Task 4 was deliberately not begun because it needed long-running implementer and reviewer subagents and the usage limit was close.

## Details

The failure mode is specific to ephemeral system directories. A handoff document exists to survive the boundary between sessions, so writing it to a location the operating system treats as not surviving that boundary defeats it completely. `/tmp` and the `$TMPDIR` under `/var/folders` are attractive defaults for an agent writing a scratch file, because they are always writable and need no decision about where the file belongs. A handoff is not scratch output. The 08-15 recovery depended on the user having the prior session's tool output to paste. Without it, the file could not have been found by search. The general rule is that any artifact whose value comes in a later session must go where a later session will look.

The 10-14 recurrence makes a further point. Catching the risk at writing time ("a reboot can delete the file") and queuing a copy as an action item is weaker than writing to the durable path in the first place, because the action item can itself be dropped. The fix belongs where the file path is chosen, ideally in the handoff skill's default. The same day's other handoff, written straight into `~/DEV/docs/handoffs/`, shows that a durable default already exists.

The retrieval lesson is a small, reusable debugging habit. Asking for the project name instead of a path turns "where is this file" into "which tree should I look in," which the user can answer at once. The decision not to start Task 4 records a judgment about work granularity under a resource limit: a clean boundary was worth more than partial progress on a task that could not be resumed halfway.

# Closeout Gaps: Touched Repos Without STATUS Updates and Checks That Did Not Run

The 2026-10-13 closeouts on the Mac surfaced two kinds of incompleteness that a clean-looking closeout can hide. One was a repo that was touched during the day but whose `docs/STATUS.md` was not updated, which breaks the rule that every touched repo gets a STATUS update. The other was a verification step whose script was not on disk, so it did not run. The 2026-10-14 closeouts closed the first gap for Flint, found the duplicate-heading problem again in a second repo, and added a timeout hazard for the landed-ledger scan.

## Key Points

- **The STATUS rule applies to every repo touched, not only the one that was the focus.** On 10-14 Flint's audit entry, open question and handoff were pushed (`650c4ed`, `27d63a1`), and the resume-card check reported 7 projects touched with 0 gaps.
- **A missing check must be reported as not run.** `skill-portability-check.py` was absent on 10-13, and the closeout said so instead of implying the check passed.
- **Uncommitted files from another session get their own commit.** Flint's 101 foreign files became commit `9eede18`. On 10-14 Flint STATUS was again noted as shared with another session, so the rule is to run `git status` before committing there.
- **Duplicated headings break scripted edits, and this keeps happening.** "Current state" appeared twice in `ZoteroInjestion/STATUS.md` on 10-13. On 10-14 Flint's STATUS had `## Open questions` three times, and a scripted edit keyed on it failed. The fix both times was to edit only the first, current section.
- **`landed.py scan` takes longer than the 300-second tool limit.** Run it in the background with its own timeout. A first background attempt exited with code 144, which is a timeout or kill signal, not a scan result.

## Details

The first closeout on 10-13 found the gap with a simple test: a repo worked in during the session should show a changed STATUS file. Flint was worked in, and its STATUS was not changed. By the next morning's closeout that was fixed, and the card check reported zero gaps across seven touched projects. That turned the rule into a checked result instead of something left to memory.

The duplicate-heading problem is now confirmed in two repos on two consecutive days, which makes it a property of how STATUS files grow and not a one-off. Sessions add a new `## Open questions` or "Current state" block instead of editing the existing one, and any tool that finds a section by its heading text then hits several matches. "Edit the first section only" is the workaround. The structural fix is to merge the duplicate sections, or to have a check flag a repeated level-2 heading, since `where-was-i --decisions` also reads these sections. The `landed.py` timeout is similar: a check that cannot finish within the tool limit returns an error that can be mistaken for a finding. Exit code 144 has to be read as "did not complete," the same distinction as reporting a missing script as not run.

# Destructive Season-Replace Loader Fixed to Merge-by-Primary-Key (PFF_Data_Project)

On 2026-09-22 the PFF_Data_Project's `load_snapshot.py` — which syncs a DuckDB database between Mac and Windows via Parquet snapshots on Google Drive — was found to have silently deleted 12,750 Mac-only rows during a load. The rows were 2024–2025 `pff_premium` records across `video_plays`, `team_play`, `quarterback_charting`, and `rushing`. They were restored from the loader's own pre-load backup, and the loader was rewritten test-first to merge by primary key instead of replacing whole seasons. PR #4 merged to `main`.

## Key Points

- **The first verification said "it worked" and was wrong.** It compared only the 2026 season, so a loss confined to 2024–2025 was invisible; the loss surfaced later during closeout under a deeper check.
- **"Replace season" semantics are destructive whenever two machines each hold partial data.** A full-season delete-then-load assumes the snapshot is a superset of local data — false when each machine holds categories the other does not (here, Mac-only `pff_premium` rows).
- **Merge-by-PK is the safe default:** insert new rows, update matching rows, leave local-only rows alone. The dry run now reports two numbers per file — rows to add, and local-only rows kept — so the preserved set is visible before committing.
- **The loader's own pre-load backup made recovery possible** (`data/pff_before_load_snapshot_<ts>.db`); a second backup was taken before the restore, and every other table was checked for row loss.
- **Row-count verification must cover every season the load touches**, not just the newest one.
- **Rule recorded to memory: swap the Parquet files on Drive, never the `.db` file itself.**
- **Pull order matters on the other machine:** Windows must `git pull` *first* — without it, Windows runs the old destructive loader against the corrected snapshot.

## Details

The verification failure is the more transferable lesson of the two. A row-count check is only as wide as the partition it samples, and checking the season under active work is the natural, cheap, and wrong choice: the current season is the one most likely to be correct, because it is the one the snapshot was built to carry. The damage lived in the historical seasons precisely because nobody was looking there and because that is where the two machines' holdings had diverged over time. This is the same shape as the false-positive verifications catalogued in [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] and the narrow-predicate reporting in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]] — the check answered a question ("is 2026 intact?") strictly narrower than the one being asked ("did this load lose anything?"), and answered it accurately. The corrective rule is stated in scope terms rather than as a one-off fix: verification must span every partition the operation writes.

The semantic bug underneath is a distribution assumption baked into a verb. `DELETE WHERE season = X` followed by an insert is correct exactly when the incoming snapshot is a superset of what is already there — a valid assumption for a single-writer pipeline, and invalid the moment a second machine accumulates rows the first has never seen. Once two machines each hold partial data, the only non-lossy verb is merge, and merge requires a primary key to decide insert-versus-update. This mirrors the finding in [[connections/newer-is-not-more-complete]]: revisions supersede, but accumulating records diverge, and the correct verb for a diverging set is merge or append rather than replace. It is also the same trade-off that drove `/MIR` → `/E` in [[concepts/windows-backup-recovery-inventory]] — when the artifact's value is that it holds something the other side may no longer have, "make identical" is never the right operation.

The recovery path is worth preserving as a design endorsement rather than an incident detail. The loader wrote its own pre-load `.db` backup as a matter of course, and that unglamorous habit is the only reason 12,750 rows were recoverable rather than merely mourned; the session explicitly recorded "keep that behavior." Taking a second backup before the restore extended the same discipline to the repair itself — consistent with the tarball-before-destructive-git rule in [[concepts/pre-destructive-git-backup-discipline]] and the caution in [[connections/the-preservation-step-must-itself-be-verified]] that a safety net nobody checks is worse than none. Two environment notes round out the session: plain `python3` on the Mac has no `duckdb`, so the loader must run under `~/.local/bin/uv run --with-requirements requirements.txt`; and `MEMORY.md` hit its 2,500-character cap (61 over) so a line had to be shortened before the rule could be written. After restoration the Drive snapshot was re-exported for 2024 and 2025 (12 files plus full `teams` and `players`), reaching 6,693,237 rows, +12,750.

# Cloudroom Local vs Cloud Desks and the Mac-Only Stack After Windows Retirement

On 2026-10-14 Eric confirmed that Cloudroom, a tool for running agent threads on "desks," fits his routine. He had already started 42 threads by hand. In the same session he said the Windows laptop is retired and Docker is removed, so the Mac plus Google Drive is now the only working environment. That changed three earlier answers: whether to keep memsearch, when Cloudroom is used, and whether a VPS is allowed.

## Key Points

- **Data boundary:** Local desks are for work that should keep running on the Mac. Cloud desks are only for GitHub repos with no athlete data, such as PlayCalls_SuccessRate_EPA, the personal site and Signal Plays. DexaProject, GPS, VALD, force-plate work and anything on the Drive mount are never sent to Cloud.
- **Keep memsearch and Milvus Lite.** The two main problems behind a possible SQLite switch were Docker on Windows and Windows timeouts, and both are gone. The one remaining Mac lock issue is already handled by a wrapper.
- **Cloudroom is now an all-day tool.** A Cloud thread keeps running when the Mac is closed and a Local thread pauses, so Cloud desks matter more on a single laptop.
- **Staged adoption:** use Local desks only for two weeks and do lesson 1. After that, try one Cloud thread. The VPS decision comes last. Cloud servers and schedulers were approved on 2026-10-14, so self-hosting `cloudroom-core` is allowed but deferred.
- **Retirement has to reach the docs.** Memory was updated (Tier A note, its index line, two Tier B lines; PASS). `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `machine.md` and the memory-write skill still describe two machines, and `Cloudroom_Learning/MISSION.md` still lists "Windows hands-off" and "needs Baylor IT approval."

## Details

The Cloud-desk rule applies the existing destination-split policy to a new kind of execution surface. Athlete-identifiable data already lives only on Drive and never on GitHub. A Cloud desk runs code on someone else's infrastructure, so it sits with GitHub, not with the local machine. The test is simple and checkable: a repo is eligible for Cloud only if it is on GitHub and has no athlete data. Anything that reads the Drive mount fails the test automatically.

Retiring Windows removed the constraint that shaped many past decisions, which is why answers given earlier had to be checked again. The memsearch decision turned around for this reason: the case for moving to SQLite rested on Windows-only failures, and with those gone, switching would be work with no current benefit. The other effect is documentation debt. Each file that still says "both machines are active" will steer later sessions toward cross-machine handling that no longer applies. Two edit attempts on `MISSION.md`, one through a Python heredoc and one through the Edit tool, were both blocked by the permission classifier. The next attempt is to be a plain command, and only after Eric says "edit the mission." The handoff for this session was written to a macOS temp folder, which repeats a known placement mistake.

# Closing a 49-Folder Backup Manifest Coverage Gap

On 2026-09-09 a KeystoneOS daily backup run returned `status: ERROR` with two problems: the `~/.claude` repo was one commit behind GitHub (blocking its push) and 49 folders under `~/DEV` were absent from `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`. Rather than triage the 49, the user confirmed that all of them mattered — the gap was a residue of an earlier migration — and every one was added. The manifest grew from 78 to 125 entries and the backup's job count went from 28 to 76.

## Key Points

- **The gap was invisible.** Folders absent from the manifest are never backed up, and their absence produces no error that reads as urgent — only an advisory `manifest-unmanaged` class. The 49-folder hole had existed since a prior migration.
- **All 49 were added, not triaged:** 47 as git repos (working-tree capture to the CRASHBOX SSD) and 2 as plain folders (`_ARCHIVE`, `docs` — SSD copy only, no repo semantics).
- **Two stale entries were removed** (`AI_Analyst`, `token-dashboard`) after confirming both had already moved into `~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/`, leaving 125 entries. Manifest hygiene runs in both directions: adding new folders and retiring moved ones.
- **`DexaProject`'s warning was kept deliberately** — it lives on Google Drive intentionally, so its manifest complaint is an accepted permanent condition rather than a defect to silence. A separate later finding in the same day established that the *GitHub* copy of `DexaProject` still holds a patient CSV and must be deleted.
- **The `~/.claude` behind-by-one state was resolved with `git pull --rebase --autostash`,** preserving two uncommitted edits (`settings.json`, `hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh`). Backups never auto-merge by design.
- **Commits were made but not pushed** — `~/.claude` at `dc54c97` and `~/.claude/global-memory` at `38e462b` — with the push deliberately left to the next scheduled backup run.

## Details

This is the largest instance yet of the manifest-drift failure class first catalogued in [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]] (three folders) and re-observed at [[concepts/backup-error-log-recurring-failures-2026-08-16]] (five folders). The escalation from three to five to forty-nine is informative: the earlier gaps were ordinary drift from folders created faster than manifest entries, whereas this one had a single structural cause — a migration that moved or created many directories at once while the manifest, being hand-maintained, stayed where it was. Bulk moves are precisely the event a curated list cannot survive, which strengthens the standing proposal in [[concepts/dev-folder-manifest-default-deny]] to derive the manifest from a directory scan rather than maintaining it by hand. The default-deny guard did its job in that the folders were reported rather than silently excluded, but reporting alone is only sufficient when the report is acted on, and forty-nine entries accumulating across weeks shows the report being observed and deferred.

The removal of `AI_Analyst` and `token-dashboard` is the neglected half of manifest maintenance. A manifest entry pointing at a folder that has moved into `_ARCHIVE` will either fail loudly (noise) or resolve to a stale path (worse), and neither outcome is caught by any check that only asks "is every folder covered?" The `DexaProject` decision demonstrates the third state a manifest entry can occupy: an accepted, documented exception whose warning is expected output rather than a pending task. Recording the reason — it lives on Google Drive intentionally — is what prevents a future maintenance pass from either "fixing" it or being confused by it, the same discipline applied to the two large graph files kept deliberately in the 2026-09-01 classification pass. Notably, the same day's repo-visibility audit found that this deliberate local exception coexists with a genuine problem at a different layer: `erash11/DexaProject` is still a GitHub repository containing a patient CSV, awaiting deletion. A documented exception on one axis does not clear the artifact on every axis.

The `git pull --rebase --autostash` choice is worth isolating as policy. The backup job pushes several repos, and a repo that is behind its remote cannot push; the tempting resolutions are a force-push (destroys remote history) or a merge (creates a commit the operator did not author). Rebasing with autostash preserves both the remote's history and the two uncommitted working-tree edits, and the stated principle — backups never auto-merge — keeps the backup system from making content decisions on the operator's behalf. This is the same restraint shown when a two-writer SecondBrain conflict was resolved by staging both sides rather than adjudicating it, per [[concepts/stack-doctor-sweep-2026-08-11]]. The decision to commit `~/.claude` and `global-memory` without pushing follows the same logic in the other direction: the push is the backup's job, so leaving it to the next scheduled run keeps one owner for that action rather than racing it.

# SpeedProfiling Project (Baylor Football Velocity Profiling)

SpeedProfiling is a Baylor football velocity-profiling project that pulls full-game 10 Hz Catapult GPS data, aligns it with college football play-by-play (via CFBD / cfbfastR), and produces per-athlete speed/velocity profiles adapted from a workshop method authored by "Alex." The project is developed as a private R repository (`github.com/erash11/SpeedProfiling`, 176-package renv lockfile) executed against a 7-ticket implementation plan tracked in the KeystoneOS `.scratch/speedprofiling/issues/` directory, using the mattpocock `implement` and `code-review` skills. On 2026-07-18, tickets 01, 02, 04, and 07 were advanced; on 2026-07-20, ticket 05 (GPS↔play-by-play merge, on-field separation, workload tables) was closed and shipped on PR #3.

## Key Points

- **Ticket-driven, per-session workflow:** the project is decomposed into 7 tickets; each ticket is implemented in a fresh session via `/mattpocock-skills:implement <ticket path>`. The `Status:` line in each ticket file is the claim mechanism that prevents parallel-session collisions. Eric prefers fresh parallel sessions per ticket over driving all tickets from one session.
- **catapultR credentials-object API change:** the installed catapultR uses a new credentials-object API — `ofCloudCreateToken(sToken=…, sRegion='America')`; the old `token=` argument no longer exists. `R/01_get_data.R` was rewritten for this API in ticket 04.
- **Deleting a token file does not revoke it server-side:** the old 2023 Catapult token had to be revoked manually in the OpenField UI — removing the local JWT file does not invalidate the token on Catapult's servers. Ticket 02 hardened `.gitignore` against `AccessTokens.txt`/`*token*.txt` and migrated live values into `.Renviron`, but server-side revocation of a superseded token is a separate manual step (logged as an Eric-manual action item).
- **Full 10 Hz pull verified (ticket 04):** the pull retrieved 8,932,931 rows at true 10 Hz (0.1 s spacing, max velocity 20.3 mph) for all 61/61 athletes (79 MB, gitignored) plus 188 play-by-play plays; 69/69 testthat tests pass. A feasibility probe gate hard-stops before the bulk pull unless genuine 10 Hz rows with all required columns return.
- **Ticket 05 — GPS↔play-by-play alignment (2026-07-20):** merged 10 Hz GPS with play-by-play using the kickoff surge signature as a numerical time anchor, separated on-field from sideline athletes via a two-part rule (sideline boundary + metabolic-power gate), and produced per-play workload tables. Closed on PR #3. See [[concepts/speedprofiling-gps-playbyplay-alignment]].
- **Game selection is config, not code:** game selection moved from hardcoded `GAME_*` variables to a `GAMES` table in `R/config.R` (activity ID + cfbd args per row). Adding a game is a one-row config edit; an empty `GAMES` renders the activity list to pick from. Per-game `.rds` caching pays the slow pull once.
- **Stacked PRs merge in order #1 → #2 → #3;** ticket 04's PR #2 is stacked on ticket 03's PR #1.

## Details

The project adopts a set of workshop R scripts (from an author "Alex") as reference material and re-implements them ticket by ticket against Baylor's live data sources. Ticket 01 established the repo, adopted the Drive scripts/docs, and set FERPA rules in AGENTS.md with a CLAUDE.md adapter, gitignore protection, and a private repo. A standards review of the adopted scripts found four real defects — notably a timestamp-conversion bug in `01_get_data.R` and play-end windows in `02_combine_data.R` that erroneously absorb halftime gaps — which were logged to the tracker and mapped to downstream tickets 03–06 rather than patched twice in reference code. Ticket 02 decoded the Catapult JWT scopes (`connect, catapultr, sensor-read-only`, expiry 2126), confirming the sensor scope needed for the 10 Hz feasibility probe, and migrated tokens from an untracked `AccessTokens.txt` (hardened out via `.gitignore` patterns `AccessTokens.txt` and `*token*.txt`) into `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\.Renviron` (`CATAPULT_TOKEN`, `CFBD_API_KEY`). Two environment notes surfaced during setup: the local `G:\My Drive` mount is much faster for adopting workshop files than downloading them through the Drive API, and `reactablefmtr` was archived off CRAN so it must be installed from GitHub for a clean renv restore (the renv snapshot-type setting also had to be fixed for `renv::status()` to report clean).

Ticket 04 delivered the core game-data pull (8.9M rows at true 10 Hz for 61 athletes), verified end-to-end (69/69 tests, both `.rds` caches hit on re-run). The BYU game (BYU – G5 – 09.28.24) was auto-selected because ticket 02 had already verified its play-by-play and Eric was unavailable to pick interactively; swapping games is a one-row `GAMES` config edit. Ticket 04 anticipated two forward-looking findings for ticket 05: Catapult X/Y coordinates return in venue coordinates requiring a transform, and the cfbfastR `wallclock` column might simplify GPS↔play timestamp alignment. Ticket 05 (2026-07-20) resolved both — the venue-coordinate issue via PCA field-frame recovery and the timestamp alignment via the kickoff surge signature rather than `wallclock`. A recurring environment note: background R tasks can report a false "exit code 1" even when the script log shows a clean end-to-end run, so the log must be checked before assuming failure (see [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]). Ticket 03 (analysis core + tests) and ticket 07 (KeystoneOS/SecondBrain integration) were also run as parallel fresh sessions, and ticket 06 (velocity profiles — sprint detection, NLS fits, bootstrap CIs, position-group comparisons) remains downstream.

# Telemetry Export Automation via Browser Driving (telemetry_pull.py)

On 2026-09-29, after shipping PP_Recruiting workbook 015, work began on `scripts/telemetry_pull.py` — a Playwright-driven tool to automate the 22-file manual export routine that feeds the recruiting workbooks from Teamworks Telemetry. Browser automation was chosen over two rejected alternatives: a printing-press-generated API CLI (blocked by the project's own handoff rules) and the paid Teamworks API. On 2026-09-30 the tool was repaired rather than rebuilt — a scope-filter defect was fixed and pushed as `20e2de6` — and it then carried the 2023, 2024, and 2026 leaderboard pulls, including a clean 44-file 2026 load.

## Key Points

- **The API route was ruled out on policy, not capability.** The printing-press skill generates CLIs from API specs, and PP_Recruiting's handoff Rule 3 forbids touching Telemetry's auth token or internal API; the sanctioned alternative, the Teamworks API, costs money. Browser automation was the remaining option, and the 2026-09-30 session re-confirmed that the Player Traits and Advanced Stats leaderboard pages are exactly what the tool already downloads, so no new CLI was warranted.
- **Read the filter pills individually, not the wrapper.** Telemetry changed its filter box; the original code read the wrapper element, so a two-pill state came back as the single string `"Power FourFBS"`. Reading each pill separately is what makes scope assertions meaningful.
- **Additions must precede removals.** The site refuses to remove the last remaining filter pill, so `set_scope` was reordered to add FBS *before* removing Power Four. A naive "clear then set" sequence deadlocks on this rule — the same reason the "Clear" control never removed Power Four scope in the first place.
- **A hidden Chrome window is a silent download stall.** When `document.hidden` is true, screenshots freeze and CSV downloads stop after the first file — observed on 9/16 and again on 9/30, resolved both times by bringing the window forward. Three runs where Chrome exited with code 0 mid-download were attributed to the window being closed or a pending Chrome self-update, not a crash; the operating rule is to leave the tool's Chrome window alone for roughly five minutes during a run and to check for a pending "Relaunch to update" beforehand.
- **Design is defensive by construction:** elements are located by label rather than position, each downloaded file is validated (correct tab, group, row count, not a duplicate of the previous file), a manifest is written at the end, filenames follow the 2025 convention, and nothing is overwritten. The QB test file was deliberately deleted before the full run so the manifest would list every file produced by that run.
- **The position-group selector is searchable** (type, select, verify), which makes the 11-group loop reliable once the first two downloads succeed; scope and season still reset to Power Four / 2026 on every switch between the Player Traits and Advanced Stats tabs and must be re-set and re-verified per tab batch.

## Details

The decision path is the notable part: a request for a generated CLI was declined on grounds internal to the project rather than on technical grounds. The printing-press workflow builds CLIs from API specifications, so satisfying it would have required inspecting Telemetry's auth token and internal API — exactly what the project's handoff Rule 3 prohibits. With the documented alternative behind a paywall, browser automation became the choice by elimination. The 2026-09-30 repair extends that reasoning into maintenance: when the vendor changed its filter markup, the response was a targeted fix to scope handling plus a commit and push, not a rewrite. A UI-driven integration has no contract, so its failures arrive as markup changes, and the maintenance posture that follows is small localized repairs against observed breakage.

Both defects fixed on 9/30 are characteristic of automating a UI. The wrapper-vs-pill bug produced a *plausible-looking* scope string (`"Power FourFBS"`) that no assertion rejected, which is the exact failure the per-file validation exists to catch; the fix was to read the underlying individual elements rather than their container — stepping down from a convenient aggregate to the ground-truth elements. The add-before-remove ordering is a constraint of the site's own filter semantics (it will not drop to zero pills), so the automation has to encode an ordering a human operator would have discovered by trial. The Chrome-visibility findings are the most operationally important, because they make the automation's failure mode a *partial* success: the first file downloads, subsequent ones silently do not, and Chrome may exit cleanly with status 0. An exit code of 0 after an incomplete batch is therefore not evidence of success, and the manifest plus row-count checks are the only reliable completion signal — a local instance of reconciling a reported exit status against on-disk artifacts.

Validation against live data followed a graduated escalation: a QB Player Traits 2026 FBS test returned 264 rows from 138 teams, then the full pull ran. The 2023 and 2024 baseline pulls produced 44 verified files (133 teams in 2023, 134 in 2024), filed via `file_exports.py` into `_exports/2023_baseline/fbs/` and `_exports/2024_baseline/fbs/`, and the full 2026 load (FBS plus FCS and Group of Six) ran clean at 14,397 players with 1,485 flagged players meeting the snap minimum. Export scope was standardized to FBS with a Minimum Snaps 1 filter to match the 2025 exports. One scope question was left open for the user: whether the 2026 FCS pull should be FCS only or FCS plus Group of Six, to match the 2025 baseline folder named `fcs_g6` — a naming artifact of the prior year's run that now has to be interpreted rather than assumed.

# PP_Recruiting Three-Season Honors Benchmark (2023–2025)

On 2026-09-30 the PP_Recruiting honors benchmark was extended from a single 2025 season to three seasons (2023–2025) by pulling 2023 and 2024 Telemetry leaderboard exports and re-running the honors matcher. The result is 1,417 honoree player-seasons — roughly double the prior 710 — with 1,679 of 1,681 honors matched (99.9%), written to `_exports/honors/honors_benchmark_2023_2025.csv`. The expanded reference population was then placed *beside* the existing workbook 013 targets rather than replacing them, and immediately exposed several targets sitting well above what actual honorees achieve.

## Key Points

- **Scale and match rate:** 1,417 honoree player-seasons across 2023–2025 (from 710), 1,679/1,681 honors matched. The two misses were Justin Lockhart (San José State 2023, absent from Telemetry's 2023 export) and a duplicate Dylan Sampson row — a near-complete match rate whose residual is attributable to source gaps rather than matcher logic.
- **Telemetry's Team column is the season's school, not the current one.** Verified via Cam Ward 2023 → Washington State and Will Howard 2023 → Kansas State. This makes multi-season joins safe without transfer-portal correction.
- **Medians sit beside targets, not in place of them.** The user's explicit call was to show honoree medians side by side with 013's targets, preserving the existing rubric so any divergence is attributable to the reference population rather than to a changed threshold.
- **Several 013 targets exceed honoree medians,** including OT Pass Blocking 79 vs median 67, OT Stops Allowed 65 vs 41, OG Penalty 71 vs 50.5, EDGE Disruption 80 vs 65, and CB CROE 74 vs 65. Because the targets were derived from Player Impact 90+ players, either that group over-sets the bar or those metrics simply do not track honors.
- **Sample thinness bounds the conclusions:** the All-American population is too small at QB (7) and TE (6) to support per-position inference, so the benchmark is read as position-conditional and not uniformly trustworthy.
- **Defaults were set by the agent and flagged as changeable:** minimum snaps 300, and second-team All-Americans sourced from AP only. Four metric renames were applied in the build script so names match PORTAL INPUT (e.g. `EPA/Target` → `EPA Per Target`) and the SETTINGS lookups line up.

## Details

The benchmark's analytical value comes entirely from widening the reference population: with one season, a target above the honoree median could be dismissed as noise; with three seasons and 1,417 player-seasons, a target 24 points above the honoree median on OT Stops Allowed is a property of the rubric rather than of the sample. The deliberate decision to show medians *alongside* the existing targets — rather than overwriting them — is what makes that comparison legible to the people who own the thresholds, and it mirrors the discipline used in the earlier benchmark workbook, where no formula or threshold was altered so that any difference between versions was attributable to population alone. The consequence is a question that the data can frame but not settle: whether the Player Impact 90+ cohort used to derive the targets represents a genuinely higher bar than award voters apply, or whether the flagged metrics (offensive-line pass blocking and penalties, EDGE disruption, CB CROE) simply have no relationship to honors selection. That question was explicitly deferred to a conversation rather than resolved by edit.

Two methodological details matter for anyone re-running the build. First, the Team-column semantics were verified rather than assumed: Telemetry records the school the player played for *in that season*, so a multi-year join needs no transfer reconciliation — a check worth making explicitly, since the opposite convention would have silently mis-assigned every transfer's honors. Second, the choices that the matcher cannot derive from data were set as named, changeable defaults (300-snap minimum, AP-only second-team All-Americans) and recorded as such, which keeps them visible for later revision instead of hardening into unexamined behavior. Metric renaming in the build script, rather than in the workbook, keeps the lookup contract with PORTAL INPUT and SETTINGS in one place.

The expanded benchmark also surfaced a downstream screening concern. After the full 2026 load, per-position flagged counts ran far above the 30–50 range the stakeholder wanted — offensive guard at 316 and offensive tackle at 175, with running back (48) the only position inside the range — attributed to the offensive-line profile route adding names. That is the same open concern as the target-versus-median gaps, seen from the output side: thresholds that no honoree clears cannot discriminate, and a board that returns 316 names at one position is not a shortlist.

# Connection: Sports-Tech Vendor Integration Friction at Baylor

## The Connection

Baylor Athletics integrates with several major sports-technology vendors for athlete monitoring data: Catapult (GPS/load), Perch (weight room performance), Kitman (athletic training utilization), and — as of 2026-08-02 — Kinexon (volleyball player tracking). Each has surfaced a distinct integration friction pattern. Catapult's token model silently expires — documented in [[concepts/catapult-connect-api-reference]] and the broader [[connections/catapult-token-friction-across-baylor-projects]]. Perch's auth scheme worked backwards from all initial assumptions — documented in [[concepts/perch-api-integration-reference]]. Kitman offers no direct API access at all, requiring vendor mediation for every pull — documented in [[concepts/at-utilization-benchmarks-project]]. Kinexon exposes a REST API but keeps its docs, endpoints, and credentials non-public, released only through the customer success manager — documented in [[concepts/kinexon-volleyball-tracking-project]].

## Key Insight

All four vendors share a common anti-pattern: naive integration assumptions fail, and the failure is not discoverable from documentation alone — it requires empirical discovery through an actual integration attempt or, in Kitman's and Kinexon's cases, a human/contractual channel. The failure modality differs by vendor, and the appropriate strategic response is calibrated to the friction type:

- **Kitman (vendor-mediation):** no API exists at this contract tier; design for a single comprehensive, precisely-specified request rather than iterative pulls. Every field omitted costs a full vendor-mediation round trip. The access constraint is also leverage for contract renegotiation.
- **Kinexon (gated docs):** a REST API exists but its documentation, endpoints, and bearer-token credentials are non-public and released only via the CSM. The correct interim strategy is to build against the documented CSV export (aided by open-source parsers like floodlight) while awaiting CSM-provided API access — decoupling schema/dashboard work from the credential wait.
- **Catapult (silent expiry):** tokens look valid but may be silently revoked; verify token freshness actively rather than assuming validity based on format or absence of an explicit expiry error. Integration tokens (shown once, non-refreshable) differ from OAuth tokens (60-minute lifecycle) in ways not obvious from the token's appearance.
- **Perch (backwards assumption):** a token that looks truncated or broken may be valid; the expected auth scheme (`JWT`) may not be the one that works (`Bearer`). Probe the live API with multiple auth schemes rather than inferring from token format.

The meta-pattern: sports-tech vendor APIs tend to be designed for their own client workflows, not for third-party integration. Documentation does not fully describe edge cases, token lifecycle constraints, access tier limitations, or is withheld entirely behind a human gatekeeper. Treating the first integration attempt as discovery rather than production — and budgeting calendar time for empirical verification of credentials and data shape, or for a vendor round trip — is the correct methodology for any new Baylor sports-tech vendor integration. A recurring architectural response is local-first ingestion (sync CLI → local DB → dashboards, athlete data gitignored), which insulates downstream analysis from API rate limits and access uncertainty.

## Evidence

- 2026-04-25 (16:06): Perch API debugging revealed that a 63-hex-char token (which appeared truncated/broken) was valid under `Bearer` auth, while `JWT` returned 401. All other endpoint, user-list key, and pagination assumptions also proved wrong before the 436-athlete ingest succeeded.
- 2026-06-09 (17:13): AT_Utilization_Benchmarks discovered Kitman API is completely vendor-mediated — "every forgotten field in a request costs a full round trip." 17 months remain on the contract; paying license fees while needing vendor mediation for one's own data is framed as contract-renegotiation evidence.
- 2026-06-10 (17:39 and 18:30): Catapult Connect v6 API reference documents that "integration tokens are shown once and non-refreshable vs. 60-min OAuth tokens." The same day, a Tezino sync failed because a token minted 2026-05-13 was silently revoked despite appearing valid.
- 2026-08-02 (16:58): Kinexon Volleyball scaffolding confirmed the REST API's docs/endpoints/credentials are non-public and CSM-gated; an email request was sent ~2026-08-01 and became the project's sole blocker, with a CSV-export interim path adopted to keep schema/dashboard work moving.

# Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology

On 2026-05-21, a structured 7-day retrospective (covering May 14–21) and a cold-project triage exercise were conducted to address project sprawl across many concurrent initiatives. The retrospective produced a structured cross-project summary of work completed and 7 open loops with next actions; the triage sorted cold projects into 4 buckets and shipped a decision-tracking HTML artifact at `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html`.

## Key Points

- **7-day retrospective format:** a structured recap of all projects touched in a rolling window, categorized by status, covering CLI development (Zotero, Catapult), 5 new skills installed, Fireflies setup, memory and Obsidian integration, token dashboard setup, and side fixes for May 14–21. Concluded with 7 identified open loops, each paired with a concrete next action.
- **Cold-project 4-bucket triage:** cold projects (not touched during the retrospective window) are sorted into: **Resume** (active work, blocked on a specific next action), **Decide** (uncertain whether to continue; needs a deliberate go/no-go decision), **Done** (formally closeable), **Archive/Kill** (permanently deprioritized or abandoned). The 2026-05-21 run sorted 16 projects: 3 resume, 2 decide, 3 done, 8 archive/kill.
- **Triage output artifact:** `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html` — a self-contained HTML file summarizing all bucketed projects with statuses and next actions, usable offline without re-running the triage.
- **Hottest cold project:** `Risk_Stratification_Engine` was flagged as the highest-priority cold project to resume next.
- **Project sprawl as a recurring pattern:** the user explicitly noted difficulty maintaining orientation across many concurrent initiatives; periodic retrospectives and triage dashboards were identified as the structural remedy.

## Details

The retrospective was triggered by the user explicitly losing track of what had been started, stopped, or left mid-flight — a common failure mode when many parallel workstreams run simultaneously across different tools, repositories, and roles. Rather than relying on memory or ad-hoc review, the session generated a structured cross-project summary covering the prior 7 days, making the "what exists and where it stands" question answerable in a single, deliberate pass. The format mirrors a lightweight sprint retrospective: scope (what was touched), status (done vs. in-flight vs. blocked), and open loops (concrete next actions, not vague intentions).

The 4-bucket triage model is designed to force explicit decisions rather than letting cold projects accumulate indefinitely in an ambiguous "maybe later" state. **Resume** identifies projects with a clear next action that are still worth pursuing. **Decide** surfaces projects that need a deliberate go/no-go call rather than being quietly ignored — the act of naming these forces a decision that passive neglect defers indefinitely. **Done** provides a formal closure signal for work that is genuinely complete but hasn't been officially closed. **Archive/Kill** handles deliberate deprioritization — not forgotten, but explicitly moved out of active consideration. The HTML artifact makes the triage durable and reviewable without accessing the session that produced it; sharing it as a file also separates the "what was triaged" question from the "what should I do next" question, allowing the artifact to be reviewed asynchronously.

The retrospective also surfaced a secondary benefit: completing deferred follow-up work from prior sessions. Specifically, the Zotero CLI's `sync --full` verification — left pending after the v0.1 slash command was registered on 2026-05-19 — was completed during the retrospective, with 2,064 items ingested successfully in ~75 seconds. Catching and completing loose ends like this is a natural output of a structured retrospective: open loops that were "almost done" become clearly visible and easy to close within the retrospective session itself.

# Extracting Gated Wistia Course Videos with yt-dlp

On 2026-09-24, a transcript and summary were extracted from a gated, Wistia-hosted course video ("Lab 3A: Kaigi Meeting Structure," from the Oldbull Performance *Running the Room* course) that offered no captions, no transcript option, and no direct file download. The working pattern turned out to be `yt-dlp` addressed with a `wistia:<id>` pseudo-URL, where the ID is read off the embedded player rather than the page URL. The session produced two artifacts — a timestamped machine-generated transcript draft and a summary — under `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\Codex\2026-09-24\can-x20\outputs\`.

## Key Points

- **A browser session cannot transcribe a video.** The Codex browser connection gives visual inspection only — no audio channel — and the Wistia player exposed neither caption tracks nor a transcript control, so there was no in-browser path to the content.
- **Chrome's built-in media download fails on streaming players.** Two attempts returned "Check internet connection," which is a misleading error: the player serves a streaming playlist rather than a direct MP4, so there is no single file for the browser to fetch.
- **The working invocation uses a Wistia pseudo-URL, not the page URL:** `.\yt-dlp.exe -f "best[ext=mp4]" -o "Lab 3A - Kaigi Meeting Structure.%(ext)s" "wistia:xc103yobe7"` — 247.62 MiB downloaded successfully. The standalone `yt-dlp.exe` was used on Windows, requiring no Python environment. The ID (`xc103yobe7`) must be pulled from the embedded player markup; the course page URL does not contain it.
- **Files downloaded via PowerShell never appear in Chrome's download history.** Verification belongs in File Explorer, not `Ctrl+J`; the failed browser-download entries still sitting in Chrome history were unrelated leftovers and actively misleading as evidence.
- **A page-notes summary is not a video summary.** The first summary produced was synthesized from the lesson's written notes rather than the video's spoken content; the corrective rule is to state explicitly which source an artifact summarizes.
- **Machine transcripts are drafts.** The generated transcript contains speech-recognition errors and must be cleaned before the Kaigi content is used for anything staff-facing. Where the host *does* ship caption tracks, the next day's Sportsmith session showed the stronger option: diff an independent ASR pass against the vendor captions instead of cleaning a single transcript by eye.

## Details

The escalation path in this session is the reusable part. Three access tiers were tried in order of decreasing convenience: watch/transcribe in the browser (impossible — no audio, no captions), use the browser's native media download (fails on streaming playlists), and finally reach past the browser entirely with a dedicated downloader. The two rejected alternatives at the third tier were screen recording with system audio and simply asking Oldbull for the source file or caption track; `yt-dlp` was chosen because it needs no real-time capture and no counterparty response. This is the same substitute-a-primitive move that recurs whenever an intermediate layer is unreliable: rather than debugging why Chrome reports a connection error, drop to a tool that speaks the streaming protocol directly.

Two of the session's lessons are about evidence rather than extraction. Chrome's download history is scoped to Chrome's own downloads, so a file fetched by a PowerShell-invoked binary is invisible there — and because the earlier failed browser attempts *did* leave entries, the history actively suggested failure after the download had already succeeded. The correct check is the filesystem. Similarly, the first summary was drawn from the lesson's written page notes, which read as plausibly on-topic but describe a different artifact than the video; labeling the provenance of a summary ("this summarizes the page notes" versus "this summarizes the audio") is what makes the distinction visible to a downstream reader. Both are instances of verifying at the layer that owns the state rather than at a convenient surface that merely appears to report on it.

The draft-transcript caveat was the piece that got operationalized next. On 2026-09-25, a Sportsmith course whose player *did* expose captions was processed with a dual-transcript workflow — an independent `yt-dlp`/ASR transcript compared against the site captions, with the comparison report saved as an artifact and unresolved terms flagged rather than guessed (see [[concepts/course-video-transcript-verification-pipeline]]). Read together, the two sessions define a fallback ladder for gated course media: prefer two independent derivations and diff them; where only one exists, as here, ship it explicitly labeled as a draft.

## Related Concepts

- [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] — Chrome's download history and a page-notes summary are both intermediate surfaces that misrepresent the underlying artifact; the fix in each case is to check the ground truth (the filesystem, the audio).

# Connection: A Killed Process Leaves Debris That Blocks the Retry

## The Connection

A process that is killed rather than exiting does not run its cleanup path, and what it leaves behind is invisible, persistent, and hostile to the next attempt. On 2026-09-11 an OOM-killed memsearch index left a stale lock file naming a dead PID — and a second such lock, orphaned since August 5, was still present, meaning the condition had silently persisted for over a month. On 2026-07-27, in-session reindex tasks killed twice left orphaned indexer processes holding CPU, requiring manual cleanup. The common finding, stated on 2026-09-11: dead-PID locks are not self-healing.

## Key Insight

The debris is worse than the failure that produced it, because the failure is loud and the debris is silent. An OOM kill is visible — the run stops, the step's duration is anomalous, the operator notices. The lock file it leaves is a small, syntactically valid artifact that the next run reads as a legitimate signal meaning "another indexer is working," so the next run declines politely and logs nothing alarming. The failure mode therefore inverts: a loud crash becomes an indefinitely quiet no-op, and the system reports normal operation while doing none of the work. That one lock survived from August 5 through at least 2026-09-11 is the proof that nothing in the ordinary cycle repairs this; the condition accumulates until someone explicitly checks whether the PID named in the lock is alive.

The structural fix, which none of these cases yet implement, is that any guard file naming a process must be validated against that process's existence before being honoured. A lock is an assertion about the world — "PID 41234 holds this resource" — and assertions about the world go stale exactly when the world moves without notifying the assertion's author. This is the same reasoning that makes an install-time path capture rot silently, and the same reasoning that makes a preservation step require its own verification: a mechanism whose whole purpose is to protect a later operation must be checked, because an unchecked safety net is worse than none. The archive-collision overwrite from 2026-09-09 makes the point from the other direction — there the debris was not a lock but a destroyed file, produced by a cleanup step that assumed a precondition (one archive per day) nothing enforced.

The operational corollary is short: after any kill, enumerate what the killed process owned. Locks, temp files, child processes, partial writes. The kill notification tells you the parent is gone; it tells you nothing about what the parent was holding.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-11 (13:10): the OOM-killed backup left a stale memsearch lock; a second lock orphaned since August 5 was found alongside it. Both would have blocked the next run and were cleared manually, with the explicit lesson recorded that dead-PID locks are not self-healing.
- 2026-07-27 (16:40): foreground memsearch reindex tasks killed twice, each time leaving orphaned indexer processes still consuming CPU that required a manual cleanup pass — a killed parent does not guarantee clean teardown of its children.
- 2026-09-09: a `cp` into a date-keyed archive path destroyed three prior `.errors.log` lines because the cleanup step assumed at most one archive per day; recovered only because git happened to hold a second copy.
