- [[concepts/cfb-victory-model-evaluation]] - Earlier forecast-evaluation work on judging a model honestly before trusting it.
- [[concepts/codex-adversarial-verification]] - The Codex review pattern used for the Phase 2 re-review.
- [[concepts/transient-vendor-slowness-retry-the-page-not-the-run]] - The per-request retry pattern the CFBD client lacks.
- [[concepts/api-key-entry-hidden-prompt-not-placeholder]] - The key-entry lesson from the first real-data run.
- [[concepts/do-not-invent-facts-in-status-notes]] - Why the unclear "approved to send" was held instead of read as permission.

Side session (23:00): Baylor 2026 scratch read, decision not to keep the scratch DB, partial-week bug sent to the Phase 3 session. Phase 3 session (23:00): six tasks built, review fixes, 291 tests, week-5 connection drop, "approved to send" left unanswered.

# Resumable Pull Marked a Partial Week Complete

In the CFB_Playoff_Benchmarks resumable weekly pull, a week was treated as "done" once any of its plays were stored. On 2026-10-16 a side session pulled 2026 week 7 while only the Thursday games had been played. Under that rule the week was marked complete, so the pull would never return for the Saturday games. In a weekly scheduled job this loses games every week, and nothing reports an error.

## Key Points

- **The completion test was coarser than the unit of work.** The pull fetches by week, but games finish at different times within a week. "Any rows exist" therefore measures that the week has started, not that it is finished.
- **The fix keys completeness on each game:** a week counts as missing when any completed game in it has no plays or no drives.
- **The regression test is one week with two finished games, only one of them stored.** The pull must treat that week as incomplete.
- **The bug was found in a side session and sent to the original Phase 3 session** to fix in Task 6. The message was queued with no reply channel, so the merge checklist includes confirming the fix and its test landed.

## Details

Resumable pipelines save cost by skipping work already done, and the skip test is where they go wrong. Testing for the presence of any row is cheap and right for the common case, a week pulled after all its games are over. It fails in the one case that matters for a live season, a pull run mid-week. The failure is also permanent: once the marker says done, no later run looks again. That makes it worse than a crash, which at least gets retried. The general rule is that a completion marker has to be computed at the grain where completion actually varies, here the individual game. It also has to be checked against an external list of what should exist (completed games), not inferred from what was stored.

This is the same family as the DuckDB loader that checked only the 2026 season and missed losses in 2024–2025. In both, a check confirmed something narrower than the question being asked. The side session saw the bug because its scratch database held a partial week 7, which is also one reason that copy was not kept: stale partial state is exactly what feeds this bug. The first real weekly run of Phase 3 is the place to confirm the fix, by checking that weeks 1–6 match the scratch read.

# Tests Writing Into the Real Project Folder Overwrote a Run Receipt

During the Phase 3 build of CFB_Playoff_Benchmarks on 2026-10-16, it turned out that some tests wrote into the project's real `logs/` folder. Some of that output leaked to Google Drive through the snapshot path. One test run overwrote the real Phase 2 success receipt, `logs/last_run_phase2.json`. The fix made every test run inside its own temp folder. This was the last fix on the branch, and it was committed and pushed with 291 tests passing.

## Key Points

- **A test that writes to real paths can destroy evidence.** The overwritten file was a receipt, the artifact that records a real run succeeded. After the leak it described a fake-data test run.
- **Default to a temp folder per test,** and route every write location (logs, receipts, Drive snapshot target) through configuration the tests can redirect.
- **Check new projects for this as a standing item.** It was recorded as a lesson to apply beyond this repo.
- **Recovery is cheap here but has to be done:** re-run Phase 2 without `--pull-sp`, which costs 0 API calls.
- **Cleanup was partly blocked.** The assistant was not allowed to delete some leaked test folders, so they were left for the user.

## Details

The project already had a receipt-integrity problem, which makes this leak worse. One of the Codex Phase 2 findings that day was that a backup failure in `run_phase2.py` left the old success receipt in place, so the receipt could claim success that never happened. The test leak damaged the same file from another direction, by replacing a real receipt with a test's. A receipt is only useful if exactly one writer, the real run, can produce it. Tests that share its path break that.

Writing to real paths is easy to miss because the tests still pass. The test asserts on what it wrote and does not notice that it wrote it somewhere shared. Isolating each test in a temp folder fixes this. It also exposes any code that hardcodes a path instead of taking it from configuration, because that code will now fail. A related note from the session: the full suite takes about 2 minutes, so it runs in the background, and the result should be read from the actual output, not from an early "completed" notice.

# API Key Entry: Hidden Prompt, Not a Placeholder One-Liner

On 2026-10-16 a new CFBD API key for CFB_Playoff_Benchmarks failed with a 401 on its first use. The `.env` file held the literal text `PASTE_KEY_HERE`. The user had been given a one-line example command and ran it as written, without replacing the placeholder. A hidden-input prompt (`read -rs`) that writes the typed value straight into `.env` fixed it. One cheap call then confirmed the key worked and had 1,000 calls left.

## Key Points

- **Users run example commands exactly as given.** A one-liner with a placeholder is a command that runs successfully and stores the wrong value, so the mistake only shows up later as an auth failure.
- **Use a hidden prompt.** `read -rs` asks for the value, does not echo it, and leaves no placeholder to forget.
- **Keys go straight into `.env`, never into chat,** because chat history is saved. This was recorded as a decision, not a preference.
- **Check a new key with one cheap call before a long run.** That call confirms the key and reports the remaining budget (here, 1,000).

## Details

A 401 suggests a bad or revoked key, and the obvious next step is to request another one. Here the key was never stored at all. Reading `.env` would have shown that immediately, which is a reminder to check what the system actually holds before blaming the vendor. The same pattern appeared earlier with the Typesafe key, where "saved EMPTY" referred to a different storage location than the one the code read.

The validation call matters more than usual for this project. Its Phase 1 runner does not resume, so a key that fails partway through a 95-call run throws away calls already spent. Spending one call to confirm the key and see the budget is cheap protection before a run that cannot be continued from where it stopped.

# Stuck Google Drive FUSE Mount: Backup Offline Errors and Hanging Readers

On 2026-10-15 and 2026-10-16 the Mac's daily backup failed with `backup-target-offline:GoogleDrive/_MACHINE`. The local Google Drive mount, a FUSE file layer that shows Drive as a folder, was stuck and did not show `_MACHINE/Backups`. While stuck, any script reading Drive hung: `landed.py scan` and `where-was-i.py --decisions` both had to be stopped and skipped at closeout. This confirms the existing Tier A note `drive-fuse-read-hang`. The same day a storage rulebook, `~/.claude/STORAGE.md`, was written to tell agents where each kind of file belongs.

## Key Points

- **A stuck mount hangs readers; it does not make them fail.** Scripts that list or read Drive block with no error. Without a timeout, a closeout step simply never returns.
- **The backup error points at the mount, not the backup.** `backup-target-offline` here means the local Drive view is stale. The files were reachable through the API, which was used to upload 5 backup files to `_MACHINE/Backups/gws-upload-2026-10-16/`. The code rsync to Drive also finished OK at 16:10.
- **The `.errors.log` entries were kept on purpose,** because the cause was not fixed. They are to be cleared only after a backup succeeds.
- **The open decision is in STATUS:** wait overnight for the mount to recover (recommended), or change the backup to write straight to Google's server instead of the local mount (option 2). The next-morning check is `ls ~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My\ Drive/_MACHINE`. If `Backups` shows, run `/backup`.
- **Suggested hardening:** a timeout or Drive-offline guard in `landed.py` and `where-was-i.py`.

## Details

Two access paths to the same Drive behaved differently. The API worked: the README fix, closing the Gemini plan and the backup upload all went through it. The FUSE mount did not. Backups and closeout scripts that depend on the mount inherit its health without any sign of it in their own errors, so a backup that looks like it lost its destination is really a local view that stopped updating. Option 2 removes that dependency for backups by writing through the path that was working. The other choice is to wait, on the expectation that a mount refresh will clear the condition.

`STORAGE.md` is the rule side of the same work. It is pointed to from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and allowed through the dotclaude `.gitignore` (commit `93c2d8b`), and a safety check was added to `daily-backup.ps1` (`e3f74fa`). The closeout recorded more maintenance debt. Registry drift stands at four items (`Cloudroom_Learning`, `Football/CFB_Playoff_Benchmarks`, `MacEverything`, and Drive `_ACTIVE/2026-10-10_House_Model`). `Cloudroom_Learning` is missing from the backup manifest, which causes the `manifest-unmanaged` error. 1.9 GB of temporary backup files in the session scratchpad are safe to delete. The startup sync skill also committed this session's history file into the dotclaude repo. That breaks the no-history rule, but the file was already tracked, so nothing new was exposed, and the question of how to fix the skill went to STATUS.

# Connection: Presence Is Not Completeness

## The Connection

Several pipelines decide whether work is finished by checking that something exists. A weekly pull counted a week as done once any plays were stored. A loader check confirmed the 2026 rows were present. A backup reported OK while the number of jobs it ran had dropped. On 2026-10-16 a background task reported "completed" while its output file was still empty. Each check answered "is there something?" when the question was "is everything there?"

## Key Insight

A presence check passes as soon as work starts, and a completeness check only passes when work finishes. Between those two moments, a presence check says "done" with full confidence. In a single run the gap is short and usually missed. In a resumable or scheduled job the gap becomes permanent, because the "done" state stops any later run from finishing the work. The fix is the same in every case. Compare what is stored against an independent list of what should exist (completed games, every partition the write touched, the expected job count), at the grain where completeness actually varies, before acting on the result.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-16: the CFB weekly pull marked a Thursday-only week 7 complete, so its Saturday games would never be pulled. The fix checks each completed game for plays and drives.
- 2026-10-16: a background task reported "completed" early with an empty output file. The lesson recorded was to wait for the real output before acting.
- 2026-09-22: the DuckDB loader's 2026-only row check passed while 12,750 rows from 2024–2025 had been deleted.
- Backup runs with `status: OK` and a single-digit job count meant the SSD was absent, not that everything was backed up.

# Closeout Gaps: Touched Repos Without STATUS Updates and Checks That Did Not Run

The 2026-10-13 closeouts on the Mac surfaced two kinds of incompleteness that a clean-looking closeout can hide. One was a repo that was touched during the day but whose `docs/STATUS.md` was not updated, which breaks the rule that every touched repo gets a STATUS update. The other was a verification step whose script was not on disk, so it did not run. The 2026-10-14 closeouts closed the first gap for Flint, found the duplicate-heading problem again in a second repo, and added a timeout hazard for the landed-ledger scan. On 2026-10-16 the same two checks did not run for a different reason: a stuck Drive mount made them hang.

## Key Points

- **The STATUS rule applies to every repo touched, not only the one that was the focus.** On 10-14 Flint's audit entry, open question and handoff were pushed (`650c4ed`, `27d63a1`), and the resume-card check reported 7 projects touched with 0 gaps. On 10-16 the card checks again reported no gaps (4 projects in one closeout, 3 in another).
- **A missing or hung check must be reported as not run.** `skill-portability-check.py` was absent on 10-13. On 10-16 `landed.py scan` and `where-was-i.py --decisions` hung on the stuck Drive FUSE mount, were stopped and skipped, and were queued to re-run once Drive reads work again.
- **Uncommitted files from another session get their own commit.** Flint's 101 foreign files became commit `9eede18`. On 10-16 another session committed and pushed this session's STATUS and handoff (`8345b3a`). Check `git log` before assuming your own files are unpushed.
- **Duplicated headings break scripted edits, and this keeps happening.** "Current state" appeared twice in `ZoteroInjestion/STATUS.md` on 10-13. On 10-14 Flint's STATUS had `## Open questions` three times, and a scripted edit keyed on it failed. The fix both times was to edit only the first, current section.
- **`landed.py scan` can outlast the tool limit for two separate reasons:** its scan takes longer than 300 seconds (exit 144 on 10-14), or it hangs on a stuck Drive mount (10-16). Both call for a timeout or Drive-offline guard in the script.

## Details

The first closeout on 10-13 found the gap with a simple test: a repo worked in during the session should show a changed STATUS file. Flint was worked in, and its STATUS was not changed. By the next morning's closeout that was fixed, and the card check reported zero gaps across seven touched projects. That turned the rule into a checked result instead of something left to memory.

The duplicate-heading problem is now confirmed in two repos on two consecutive days, which makes it a property of how STATUS files grow and not a one-off. Sessions add a new `## Open questions` or "Current state" block instead of editing the existing one, and any tool that finds a section by its heading text then hits several matches. "Edit the first section only" is the workaround. The structural fix is to merge the duplicate sections, or to have a check flag a repeated level-2 heading, since `where-was-i --decisions` also reads these sections. The `landed.py` timeout is similar: a check that cannot finish within the tool limit returns an error that can be mistaken for a finding. Exit code 144 has to be read as "did not complete," the same distinction as reporting a missing script as not run.

The 10-16 hang shows that both Drive-reading checks depend on the health of the mount, so an infrastructure fault turns into a closeout fault. The closeout correctly reported them as skipped instead of as clean, and still signed off. That is the right call only because the skipped checks were named along with the condition for re-running them. The same day's closeout also recorded a lesson about concurrency: with several sessions committing and pushing the same repos, "my changes are unpushed" has to be checked against `git log`, not assumed from memory of the session.

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.
